item.title: If it works in India, it can work anywhere: TDK Ventures’ Nicolas Sauvage on building deeptech for the world
item.description: At TechSparks 2026, the Founder and President of TDK Ventures said Indian deeptech founders should plan for international markets from the start, and use the country’s tough operating conditions to develop capabilities that customers elsewhere would value.
item.content:encoded:
For years, India’s best scientists left for the US. Now they are staying, and more of them are choosing startups over corporate labs. For Nicolas Sauvage, Founder and President of TDK Ventures, those two shifts are the biggest changes in Indian deeptech over the past five to 10 years.

“The best talent starts to go into the startups in deeptech, and they try things that they would not have tried 10 years or even five years ago,” Sauvage said in a fireside chat with Shivani Muthanna, Senior Director – Strategic Content & Video at YourStory, at TechSparks 2026.

TDK Ventures is the corporate venture capital arm of Japanese electronics company TDK Corporation. Set up in Silicon Valley in 2019, it opened its Bengaluru innovation hub in 2023, its first office outside the US. India is its second largest market by number of investments, Sauvage said.

The ecosystem he is betting on is growing. India is home to more than 4,200 deeptech startups, which raised $2.3 billion in 2025, up 37% from the year before, according to a Nasscom–Zinnov report.

During the session titled ‘Global by design: What Indian deeptech needs to become globally iconic’, he laid out what Indian founders need to get right to build companies that compete globally, from picking a first customer and the right investors to planning for scale before it becomes expensive to do so.

Where India has the right to win

Speaking on investing in SpaceTech, Sauvage named the US, China, and India as the three countries where he would consider investing as a VC. Space is one area where he believes India has a clear advantage, built on decades of institutional investment through the Indian Space Research Organisation. The government’s space promotion agency, IN-SPACe, projects that India’s space economy will grow from $8.4 billion to $44 billion by 2033, raising its share of the global market from 2% to 8%.

TDK Ventures co-led a $20.5 million Series A in Bengaluru-based spacetech startup Ethereal Exploration Guild (The Guild), which is developing a fully reusable medium-lift launch vehicle.

Sauvage also pointed to a shift in AI. The conversation, he said, has moved from tokens and compute to electrons and gigawatts, which means everything involved in delivering power to chips now matters. TDK Ventures invested in C2i Semiconductors, a Bengaluru startup founded in 2024 by former Texas Instruments engineers that builds power management technology for AI data centres. Germany’s Infineon Technologies announced the acquisition of C2i in August 2026 and completed it in October, about two years after the startup was founded.

Beyond individual sectors, Sauvage credited a cultural trait: jugaad, or resourcefulness under constraint.

“Think about the entrepreneurship journey. It means going from an idea with massive constraints and creating something that’s valuable and does a job. That sounds like jugaad to me,” he said.

That resourcefulness shows up in the numbers, he added. Capital efficiency among Indian portfolio companies is world class. “I’m from Europe, but don’t talk about Europe when we think about capital efficiency,” he said.

Let the first market shape the product

When asked what founders building from India for the world should think about first, Sauvage pointed to Exponent Energy. Founded in 2020 by former Ather Energy executives Arun Vinayak and Sanjay Byalal, the company offers 15-minute fast charging. In June 2026, TDK Ventures co-led a Rs 200 crore ($21.1 million) round in Exponent, taking the company’s total funding since 2020 to $65.7 million.

Exponent’s long-term goal was megawatt-scale fast charging for intercity buses. It could not start there. Instead, it began by supplying battery management systems (BMS) to three-wheeler makers, a fragmented market with more than 70 manufacturers at the time.

“There was no way a German startup would convince BMW to take their solution. No way a US startup would convince General Motors to take their BMS solution,” Sauvage said.

India’s fragmented market let Exponent deploy across many manufacturers in Bengaluru and beyond, giving it a base to build from.

Founders need superpowers, and so do their investors

Sauvage described founders as superheroes. Each needs a superpower: something they know or can do that no one else can. That is what draws investors in. But, like any superhero film, there are many battles before the end, and founders need allies.

“You want to make sure that the investors you pick as an entrepreneur bring the right superpower at the right time,” he said.

Corporate VCs can bring a go-to-market channel, an early anchor customer, a hard-to-access supplier, or help reducing scientific risk, depending on who they are. He urged founders to choose investors based on what they add that the cap table does not already have.

For TDK Ventures, that means drawing on TDK’s work in energy, sensing, passive components, and power supplies. Sauvage said electric motorcycle maker Ultraviolette now gets components typically reserved for TDK’s largest customers, while TDK is working with The Guild on future component requirements and roadmaps.

Alongside seeking venture-capital financial returns, he said, TDK Ventures looks for ways TDK’s capabilities, or “superpowers”, can accelerate and de-risk a founder’s journey towards building a globally significant company.

First principles over trade-offs

Sauvage traced several portfolio wins back to first-principles thinking. TDK Ventures invested in AI chip company Groq in 2020. During an interview with founder Jonathan Ross before investing, Sauvage noticed that every answer, from setting company values to hiring, firing, and designing the compiler, came back to first principles.

That approach produced a chip architecture designed around the compiler, which allowed for fully predictable, low-latency inference. Sauvage said he was convinced inference was the future before the ChatGPT moment, when he estimated the market for inference alone at more than $60 billion. In December 2025, NVIDIA signed a non-exclusive licensing deal for Groq’s technology, reportedly worth about $20 billion, and hired Ross and several members of his team.

He applied the same lens to engineering decisions that look like trade-offs. Ultraviolette, he said, uses first-principles engineering to pursue improvements in performance, weight and cost together. The company now sells its bikes in Germany, France, Switzerland, the UK, and other European markets, bringing its products into markets served by established manufacturers such as BMW. Ultraviolette recently raised $85 million in a round led by Yali Capital and TDK Ventures.

Patience and impatience at the same time

Deeptech founders, Sauvage said, need both. “Overnight success takes 10 years,” he said, noting that Groq took 10 years and SpaceX took 17. At the same time, founders need urgency and a sense of contribution to society.

Before investing, he looks for four things: a founder with a superpower, a category-defining product, a large enough market, and evidence the company can win one customer and then the next while staying capital-efficient. Markets worth $1 billion to $2 billion can be too small for the venture returns TDK Ventures seeks, he said, because the firm looks for each investment to have the potential to return the entire fund.

He cited SPAN, a Silicon Valley company led by Indian-origin founder Arch Rao. SPAN began by redesigning the home electrical panel, a product largely unchanged for a century.

As AI infrastructure demand surged, SPAN extended its power-management technology into distributed compute through partnerships, which Sauvage said changed the company’s trajectory.

Longer cycles also explain why India needs more corporate investors now, he argued. Using a roughly four-year journey to success in SaaS and fintech as an illustration, Sauvage described an ecosystem that can recycle entrepreneurial experience about 2.5 times a decade, as founders and employees carry what they have learned into new companies. A ten-year deeptech journey allows only one such cycle over the same period. Networks of repeat founders and alumni-founded businesses, like those associated with PayPal and SpaceX, therefore take longer to develop. Corporate investors can help bridge that gap with technical expertise, suppliers and customer relationships.

“I want global companies, corporates, and their corporate VCs to know this is the time to invest in India for deeptech,” he said.

Build for scale before it gets expensive

Sauvage emphasised thinking about scale and international expansion early, because shortcuts taken to win the first market in India can become expensive to reverse later.

When TDK Ventures met Ultraviolette, the team was already deliberate about Europe while focused on winning in India first, with customers riding its bikes as far as the Himalayas.

His advice to founders: find what is specific to India that a global customer would trust. India’s wide temperature range, for example, could favour energy storage that performs across extremes, such as sodium-ion or thermal batteries.

“Try to think about what makes you being in India a proof point that because you’re successful in India, you will win everywhere,” he said.

For Sauvage, India’s deeptech opportunity rests on more than talent. The founders most likely to build iconic companies are those who treat India as a starting point rather than a boundary, pick investors who fill specific gaps, and design for international markets before shortcuts become costly to undo. It is a long game that demands patience and impatience at once, and in his view, the moment for global capital to back it in India has arrived.

item.title: VeloDB’s Nitin Waghulde on why AI agents break down after the demo
item.description: At TechSparks 2026, VeloDB’s Regional Director for APAC explained why AI agents that work in pilots struggle in production, and why the fix often lies in the database underneath them.
item.content:encoded:
AI agents tend to look good in a pilot. The scope is narrow, the data is controlled, and the questions are predictable. Production is different, and that gap is where many projects stall.

Gartner predicts that over 40% of agentic AI projects will be cancelled by the end of 2027, due to escalating costs, unclear business value, or inadequate risk controls. For Nitin Waghulde, Regional Director, APAC at VeloDB, a large part of the problem sits below the model, in the data layer.

In a keynote titled ‘AI agents at scale: Surviving beyond the demo’, Nitin explained how AI agents use data differently from people, what they need to work reliably at scale, and how companies are redesigning their data infrastructure to support them.

Nitin started his session with an example. In a traditional system, a business manager who wanted last year’s sales figure would run a ready-made report and get the number in one lookup.

Ask an AI agent why sales dropped over the last three quarters, and the work changes. The agent pulls order records from the ERP and CRM systems, scans support tickets and chats to check whether major customers have escalated problems, and reads sales team reports on territory dynamics. If its reasoning is incomplete, it goes back for more.

“What used to be completed in one simple lookup or one simple query, now you’re taking hundreds of lookups for the same thing,” he said.

AI is now a customer of your data

In the past, people and reports were the main consumers of business data, and systems were built around fixed reports with clear boundaries. 

Now, Nitin said, AI has become a new customer of that data, and it behaves very differently.

Agents run around the clock, ask many questions at once, and work in an iterative loop: ask, think, search, and retry until they can answer. Their questions are also unscripted. That puts a heavy, unpredictable load on the data layer.

The challenge grows because business data lives in several places at once: transactional records, chat memory, documents, dashboards and pre-built reports, and vector stores for meaning-based search. An agent has to search all of them and combine the results before it can answer.

Each extra trip to the data adds cost. If the data is stale, the answer is wrong. Nitin compared it to driving with an inaccurate traffic map. And when data comes from many sources, it becomes harder to know where an answer came from, which creates a trust problem.

He likened it to sending someone to five filing cabinets to collect pieces of paper. By the time the person returns from the fifth cabinet, the information from the first may already be out of date.

What production agents need

Nitin outlined four requirements for agents to move from pilot to production.

  • Access to every data type: Agents need numbers from structured records, text from documents, and meaning from unstructured sources.
  • Scale: A single query may now need to scan petabytes of data, not the few terabytes that systems were once designed for. Also, the platform should support concurrency at scale to support iterative querying for data-hungry agents
  • Freshness: Agents can only act correctly on current information. If an agent processing a refund cannot see the latest transaction record, it has to wait. Every change, including updates and deletions, needs to be visible to the agent immediately, without waiting for a nightly batch job.
  • A record of every interaction: Every AI interaction leaves a trail. These logs are growing faster than business data itself, and they feed back into decision-making.

VeloDB’s answer is a single engine that handles all of these needs. The company was founded in 2023 by the original creators of Apache Doris, an open-source real-time analytics database that became a top-level Apache Software Foundation project in June 2022. According to VeloDB, Apache Doris has more than 14,000 GitHub stars and 700 contributors, and is used by over 5,000 enterprises worldwide.

To cut down the back-and-forth trips that slow agents down, VeloDB supports hybrid queries. A single query can combine SQL, vector search, and text search, running deterministic and probabilistic searches in parallel. The result is one unified source of truth instead of scattered data.

What it looks like at scale

Nitin shared two examples of companies running this architecture in production.

The first was one of the largest crypto exchanges, with more than 120 million users, which he did not name. The exchange makes transaction data available to AI agents that retail investors can query, for example to see what positions large traders are taking on an asset. He said its agents handle about 33,000 conversations with a tail latency of around 3 milliseconds, running round the clock.

The second was MiniMax, a Chinese AI company that listed on the Hong Kong Stock Exchange in January 2026 and says it serves 212 million users in more than 200 countries. MiniMax rebuilt its logging system on Apache Doris after moving away from Grafana Loki, because logs had become a valuable source of intelligence worth keeping and querying. 

Nitin said MiniMax ingests data at 10 Gbps and can query about 10 petabytes in under two seconds, at 70% lower cost. VeloDB has separately reported that the Doris-based system now supports logs across all of MiniMax’s business lines at petabyte scale with over 99.9% availability.

The same challenges apply to early-stage startups building agents, Nitin added. VeloDB works with fintech startups that face the same scaling problems as MiniMax or the crypto exchange, just at an earlier stage.

His closing point was that agents will always ask hundreds of questions, so the infrastructure has to make each one cheap, fast, and current. 

For Nitin, scaling AI agents is less about finding a better model and more about giving agents real-time, trustworthy data from a single source. Companies that get the data layer right, he argued, can make decisions faster, reduce costs, and move their agents from pilot to production with confidence.

item.title: Vast, varied, vivid: How this art festival celebrates pan-India creativity
item.description: In this photo essay, we feature more highlights from Karnataka Chitrakala Parishath’s national art festival.
item.content:encoded:
Launched in 2014, PhotoSparks is a weekly feature from YourStory, with photographs that celebrate the spirit of creativity and innovation. In the earlier 1,030 posts, we featured an art festival, cartoon gallery. world music festival, telecom expo, millets fair, climate change expo, wildlife conference, startup festival, Diwali rangoli, and jazz festival.

The Namma Art Bengaluru national festival was held at Karnataka Chitrakala Parishath (KCP) for the second time this year (see our coverage of earlier exhibitions at this popular cultural hub here). KCP’s flagship event is the annual Chitra Santhe, regarded as India’s largest street fair for art.

India’s artistic landscape is as vast and varied as the country itself. It spans intricate visual languages of Madhubani, Warli, Gond and Pattachitra; sculptural traditions of Channapatna, Dhokra and Thanjavur; miniature painting and textile traditions, and much more.

The worlds of contemporary painting, photography, installation, and new media add new perspectives and vocabularies for art lovers. The beauty of this artistic panorama truly emerges when these creative forms are showcased together.

“Art has always served as a powerful medium of expression that transcends boundaries, connects communities, and reflects the spirit of society,” explains Shashidhara Rao, General Secretary, KCP.

A pan-India exhibition that brings traditional and contemporary art into one shared space can create a powerful visual and cultural conversation. Instead of presenting India’s art traditions as isolated regional categories, such an exhibition reveals the connections between them.

Also Read
2026 Outlook: AI, robotics, biotech, unicorns and the road ahead

As seen in this photo essay, there are recurring ideas of nature, spirituality, community, identity, mythology, and everyday life. The differences are equally important: they demonstrate the extraordinary plurality of Indian experience and the many ways in which communities have interpreted and expressed their worlds.

Bringing traditional and contemporary practices together also allows the exhibition to move beyond the idea of heritage as something belonging only to the past. Traditional art forms are living practices, continually evolving through artists, artisans and new generations.

Contemporary artists, meanwhile, frequently draw upon inherited visual languages and stories while questioning, reinterpreting and transforming them for the present. Placing these works side by side makes this continuity visible.

“In an increasingly dynamic world, the role of art in preserving heritage, encouraging dialogue, and inspiring fresh perspectives has become more significant than ever,” KCP’s Rao adds.

The Namma Art festival is thus more than a showcase of beautiful objects, as shown in this photo essay. It serves as a map of India’s cultural imagination — one in which a folk painting from one region can resonate with a contemporary installation from another, and where regional identities can coexist within a larger national story.

The experience of seeing many art forms together is also deeply democratic. It invites audiences to discover unfamiliar traditions and appreciate the knowledge embedded in craft. It creates opportunities for dialogue between artists, craftspeople, designers, collectors, students, and the wider public.

Also Read
Year in review: startups that raised big from VCs in 2025

“Our festival represents a wide spectrum of artistic approaches, mediums and regional sensibilities. Their works collectively reflect the dynamism of contemporary practice in India,” says KCP president BL Shankar.

Such a national exhibition celebrates an idea that is central to India itself: unity does not require uniformity. Its strength lies in the coexistence of many languages, histories, materials, communities and ways of seeing.

By bringing traditional and contemporary art together, the exhibition can offer audiences not simply a view of Indian art, but an experience of India — diverse, layered, evolving, and connected.

Featured artists at the KCP festival include Vivek Vadkar, AG Nellagi, Ashok Mansur, Sunil Barman, Dhiraj Balchandra Patil, and Sudha Sridhar.

Vivek Vadkar is a contemporary Indian artist renowned for his powerful and emotive oil paintings of horses in motion. His popular Seven Horses compositions draw on traditions where running horses symbolise success, victory and positive energy.

AG Nellagi is known particularly for his expressive paintings of bulls. His work draws deeply on his personal experience as a farmer and on the cultural symbolism associated with the bull, which represents strength, determination, fertility, and confidence. He has received awards and recognition from the Karnataka Lalit Kala Academy and other cultural institutions.

Also Read
How IIT Madras Incubation Cell is powering India’s next-gen deeptech startups

Ashok Mansur is a visual artist and photographer with an interest in art, history and cultural imagery. A farmer by profession, he is also known for his beautiful landscapes along with people portraits.

Sunil Barman is a self-taught artist whose paintings focus on the quiet beauty of village life in Bengal. He works primarily with fine pen-and-ink drawing layered over delicate watercolour washes. His paintings evoke nostalgia for rural life where people and nature coexist in an unhurried rhythm.

“This edition has proudly presented 150 invited artists from across India. They showcase the diverse ideas, mediums and voices that reflect the spirit of traditional and contemporary art today,” festival convener SA Vimalanathan signs off.

Now what have you done today to pause in your busy schedule and harness your creative side for a better world?

(All photographs taken by Madanmohan Rao on location at Karnataka Chitrakala Parishath.)

item.title: When code is cheap, trust is not: Inside the AI-era engineering roundtable
item.description: In a closed-door roundtable, leaders from logistics, healthcare, telecom, fintech, and e-commerce discussed where to automate, where to keep humans in charge, and why observability can no longer be an afterthought.
item.content:encoded:
AI has made writing code faster than ever, but the harder question for engineering leaders is what happens after the code is written. At a roundtable on operating engineering in the AI era, leaders from logistics, food tech, healthcare, telecom, fintech, ecommerce and higher education compared notes on scaling with AI without losing reliability, security or control. The shared view was that speed is no longer the hard part. Governing it is.

The roundtable, moderated by Ipshita Basu, brought together Manjunath Nakshathri, Head of Engineering, Mojro; Shobhit Suman, CPO, HungerBox; Pavan Kumar A T, CTO, Digii (DigiiCampus); Pranjal Nadhani, Co-founder and CTO, Cautio; Kenil Paul, VP, Technology and Solutions, 6D Technologies; Rimjhim Agrawal, Co-founder and CTO, BrainSightAI; Dhruv Rastogi, Chief AI Officer, MediAssist; Chandrakesh Pandey, Senior Vice President of Technology, Niyo Solutions Inc.; Achal Sharma, CTO, TechnoSport; Sunil Kumar, Director Engineering, Meesho; and Anshul Sharma, Director Engineering, Scaler.

The session was hosted by groundcover and Data Signals in partnership with YourStory, and was led on the host side by Paul Trebe, Head of Sales and Partnership, groundcover, and Satish Dange, Founder, Data Signals.

Where the bottleneck has moved

Participants agreed that AI has compressed build time, but the pressure has shifted downstream. When agents generate large volumes of code, the questions become who reviews it, who tests it and who monitors dozens of deployments a day. Several leaders said their teams now spend more time on design, context and governance than on writing components. Agents are only as effective as the context they receive, and few organizations yet have repository knowledge, documentation and templates in a form an agent can reliably use.

Drawing the line on autonomy

The room converged on a progressive approach. Reversible, read-only work, such as fetching data or generating reports, can go to agents with little friction. Irreversible actions, such as deleting data or running database updates, stay behind human review. Blast radius matters as much as reversibility. If a wrong call could affect end users or production systems, a person makes it.

One of the participants described a ‘four eyes’ model in which AI does the maker work of reading and analyzing, deterministic rules deliver clear yes or no outcomes, and a human signs off. Another speaker described risk scoring based on severity and occurrence, which focuses human review on medium and high criticality items. Others drew the line by specialization, letting engineers use agents freely in their own domain while production ownership stays with people who can debug at 2 AM.

That scenario also surfaced in a hopeful form. Instead of waking an engineer, an agent can investigate an incident and hand over a report by morning, leaving the decision with a human. Trust, participants said, will build gradually, much as it did with online payments, and the line will keep moving.

Accountability and the skills question

Accountability drew firm agreement: it cannot be delegated to a model. Leaders remain answerable for what agents do. AI works as an intelligence multiplier, one participant noted, which means mistakes are amplified as quickly as good decisions.

Skill erosion sparked livelier debate. Some saw a shift in skills, much as calculators changed arithmetic. Others, particularly in healthcare, worried about losing the expertise needed to judge AI output at all. One practical answer was to decide deliberately where AI drafts and where humans do.

Data control as a design decision

For telecom and healthcare leaders, data control is settled at design time. Models cannot simply run in a public cloud when regulators, tenancy separation, and residency rules apply, and one mistake can bring heavy penalties. Others stressed governance from the first stage, covering what data is ingested, what is used for training versus inference, and how it is masked or de-identified. Concerns about intellectual property and bias also led to a call to vet AI tools as rigorously as new hires.

Observability for an agentic world

Observability ran through every topic. Teams described tracing agent inputs, decisions, and handoffs so they can see why an agent acted as it did and correct it. One ecommerce team learned the cost of underinvesting: a ranking change left every dashboard green while business impact surfaced days later, and the root cause analysis took more than a week. It has since built a change ledger, lineage, a system graph, and a debugging agent that proposes ranked hypotheses.

The observability view was that it can no longer sit apart from development. Paul Trebe put it plainly: “You can no longer decouple observability from development.” Agents need context-rich data to act well, he noted, and the agents themselves must be monitored, since AI traces can run to 500,000 lines that only other agents can realistically parse.

What comes next

No one claimed a finished playbook. Open questions remain on measuring agent reliability and return on investment, protecting data and IP, and keeping engineers sharp enough to challenge what AI produces.

Still, the conversation pointed to a common direction. Give developers room to move fast, but build the guardrails first. Keep humans in charge of irreversible and high-impact calls, and widen automation as trust is earned. Several participants argued that standing still is not an option, since competitors will not wait. The real test of the AI era is less about how quickly teams can build and more about how confidently they can run what they have built.

item.title: VibeCode30 2026: The 30 AI-built products to watch from India
item.description: From healthcare and education to housing, travel, and developer tools, YourStory's inaugural VibeCode30 spotlights 30 live products showing how AI is making software development accessible to a new generation of builders.
item.content:encoded:
The next generation of technology builders may not all be software engineers. They could be students, product managers, marketing professionals, small business owners or simply individuals who understand a problem well enough to solve it.

With AI-powered coding tools lowering the technical and financial barriers to software development, more people are turning ideas into working products without conventional development teams or large budgets.

Recognising this shift, YourStory launched VibeCode30, a new initiative presented by Hostinger, at the 17th edition of TechSparks 2026 in Bengaluru. The inaugural cohort celebrates 30 AI-native products built to solve real-world problems, from simplifying house hunting and improving financial literacy to supporting healthcare professionals and making everyday business operations more efficient.

Unlike traditional startup showcases, Vibecode30 focuses on products and their builders, whether they work independently or in small teams, with or without formal coding experience.

The inaugural edition received 207 applications from across the country, including smaller centres such as Ajmer, Silvassa, Sugauli, and Thoothukudi. The final 30 products represent 19 industries and 11 cities, reflecting the range of problems that AI-native builders are addressing. Importantly, every selected product had moved beyond the prototype stage and was accessible to real users.

The cohort demonstrates that while AI can accelerate software development, understanding the problem, validating the output, and improving the product remain essential. It also shows how smaller, highly specific problems can now become viable opportunities for innovation.

Meet the VibeCode30 2026 cohort:

AjmerAstro

Built by Himanshu Dadhich in Ajmer, AjmerAstro is an AI-powered astrology platform offering personalised Vedic and KP astrology guidance in English and Hindi, with a system that remembers previous conversations.

AlgoTrips

Delhi-based Tushar Garg built AlgoTrips, an AI travel planner that creates day-by-day itineraries with live pricing for flights, hotels, activities, and transfers, allowing users to plan and book trips.

Arena

Developed by Bengaluru-based Prathik Arunkumar and Arun Kumar, Arena helps schools manage house competitions through live leaderboards, digital scoring, and real-time updates.

Beet.Health

Built by Vatsl Goswami and Shivanshi Shukla,  Beet.Health helps nutrition clinics manage appointments, payments, and meal plans while enabling clients to track their progress through a mobile app and WhatsApp assistant.

Bengaluru.rent

Created by Bengaluru-based Harshit Anand, Bengaluru.rent is a free platform where tenants anonymously share rental prices and connect directly with property owners and prospective flatmates without brokers.

Benki.tech

Developed by Sonam Rao, Avinash Narsimah, and Kumaraswamy BV in Bengaluru, Benki.tech uses a simulated panel of customers to help businesses pressure test business ideas, marketing messages, and product offerings.

Bloom UPSC

Built by Bengaluru-based former banker Guru Sasidhar Pattem, Bloom UPSC provides civil services aspirants with study materials, practice questions, answer evaluation, and video lessons in English and Telugu.

Boolean Beyond

Coimbatore-based Boolean Beyond developed BeyondSave, a WhatsApp-based platform that enables local jewellery businesses to manage customer savings schemes, payments, and balances.

ElderNest

Bengaluru-based Shubham Jain created ElderNest to help families discover and compare senior care homes across India, with information on services, pricing and admission support.

Gold Investment Monitor

Created by Surendhran Sivalingam in Coimbatore, Gold Investment Monitor analyses 24 market signals and combines them into a single verdic to help Indian households assess whether to buy gold or wait.

Holt

Built by Bhubaneswar-based Debashis Nayak, Holt is an open-source memory tool for AI coding assistants that runs locally on a developer’s machine, helping them retain project context across sessions.

IndianCoffeeBeans.com

Hyderabad-based Abhishek Thrilok built IndianCoffeeBeans.com, a searchable directory tracking more than 90 Indian specialty coffee roasters and 1,200+ coffees.

Indiccore

Developed by Sahil Gulati and his team in Gurugram, Indiccore helps civil services aspirants analyse mock-test performance, identify weaknesses, and improve examination strategies.

Madhav.live

Built by Ashish Singh Shekhawat in Bengaluru, Madhav.live lets users talk to Krishna about everyday problems and receive guidance rooted in the Bhagavad Gita, in the language they are most comfortable with.

MagicSlides.app

Created by Bengaluru-based Sanskar Tiwari, MagicSlides instantly converts topics, documents, web links, and YouTube videos into presentations, supporting more than 100 languages.

Mira

Developed by Shagun Verma and Abhaya Trivedi in Mumbai, Mira is an AI voice assistant that helps short-term rental hosts handle guest enquiries and check property availability, giving small hosts the kind of front desk usually only hotels can afford. 

NextDoor.Company

Built by Sankalp Sinha in Bengaluru, NextDoor.Company helps jobseekers discover startups hiring nearby through a map-based platform with company and employment information.

Nomira

Created by Bengaluru-based Prernaa Agarwal, Nomira is a women-first travel platform combining safety information, offline maps, travel communities, and group trips.

Orbit Research

Developed by Silvassa-based student Aditya Singh, Orbit Research combines academic research tools into a single platform for discovering papers, checking references, preparing manuscripts, and creating presentations.

Penfight

Built by Amarjeet Sarma and his Bengaluru-based team, Penfight recreates the popular school desk pen-flicking game as an online multiplayer experience.

Pretend AI

Pune-based Kareena Rogers developed Pretend AI, an iPhone app that allows users to rehearse conversations with custom AI personas through realistic text exchanges.

RayAI

Created by Reshma Budhia and Swetha Sree Kannan at Chennai-based agency Toss The Coin, RayAI helps marketing teams create campaigns, content and design assets using shared brand knowledge and workflows.

Soma

Built by Gurugram-based Saurav Singhal, Soma brings together health reports, wearable data, nutrition, and fitness information to provide personalised health insights.

TofuBofu

Hyderabad-based Arnav Neil developed TofuBofu to help B2B companies measure and improve how often AI recommends them, as buyers increasingly turn to AI for product research and decision making. 

Vitfinity

Created by Bengaluru-based Pranay Reddy and his team, Vitfinity teaches financial literacy to school children through interactive simulations and a 180-lesson curriculum.

Voqalize

Built by Sripathi Krishnan and his Bengaluru-based team, Voqalize enables enterprises to integrate multilingual conversational voice AI into software applications.

Whitefield Womania

item.content:encoded:
Dear Readers, 

AI is finding cyber flaws swiftly. But are enterprises quick enough to fix them?

Nikesh Arora, Chairman and CEO of Palo Alto Networks, raises this crucial point. He notes in a LinkedIn post that most organisations, especially the smaller ones, do not have the capacity to patch flaws at the speed needed. Arora advocates virtual patching as an interim measure and calls for a shared vulnerability clearing house and faster development of protective signatures. 

As AI agents become capable of handling everyday tasks, here’s a smart ring that promises to bring AI agents to our fingertips. 

At a private launch in Bengaluru, Aina unveiled an AI-powered ring that combines a colour display, voice commands, and gesture-based controls. The startup wants its device to become an everyday interface between users and AI agents. But can it offer enough utility to justify its Rs 47,000 price tag? 

In other news, the government has cleared 12 proposals worth over Rs 7,500 crore under the Electronics Components Manufacturing Scheme. This round of approvals adds to the momentum behind the scheme, which aims to build a domestic ecosystem for components and reduce India’s dependence on imports.

Meanwhile, MakeMyTrip has acquired a majority stake in Bengaluru-based Quick Ride, a tech-led shared mobility platform. Quick Ride connects people travelling along similar routes, enabling affordable ride pooling for everyday commute. 

Lastly, here’s a bit of weekend motivation. 

Built despite opposition, legal challenges, and questions over cost, Bihar Museum has marched into the global top 10, ahead of the Met and Louvre. For YourStory’s founder Shradha Sharma, the museum not only brings the region’s history to life, but is also a reminder of what ambition and perseverance can accomplish.

Honasa Consumer, the parent company of beauty & personal care brand Mamaearth, registered an 87% year-on-year (YoY) rise in net profit for the second quarter of the current fiscal, while revenue rose 36% driven by strong growth across categories.

Deepinder Goyal has posted a series of updates and clarifications on X amid backlash from some Indian doctors who criticised his brain-monitoring wearable Temple. Earlier, on Thursday, he posted, “We stand by our science and our methods. Each of our claims is easily verifiable by individuals and institutions alike, and you will see a lot of independent studies come up on their own when the device becomes available to use.”

item.title: (Weekly funding roundup Oct 31-Nov 6) Sharp rise in capital inflow
item.description: The total funding for the first week of November was $263 million across 23 deals, compared to just $115 million in the previous week.
item.content:encoded:
November began on a positive note for the Indian startup ecosystem with venture capital funding seeing a sharp rise, after four weeks of tepid inflow of funds.

The total funding for the first week of November was $263 million across 23 deals, compared to just $115 million in the previous week.

This week saw two key breakthroughs.

First, the total funding amount was well above $200 million. This is significant as the funds raised in the preceding four weeks were below $200 million. Second, after four weeks, the Indian startup ecosystem saw a $100-million transaction from jewellery brand GIVA.

These developments provide a big boost to the startup ecosystem, which has been struggling to raise large amounts of capital. Additionally, a potential investor slump in AI companies in the aftermath of the US mid-term elections could benefit Indian startups.

This is because much of the money is concentrated in the AI segment in the US. Now one can expect some sort of rebalancing in capital distribution with certain funds flowing into India. However, it is early days to comment on how the capital will flow into the country.

Key transactions

Jewellery brand GIVA raised $100 million led by Multiples Alternate Asset Management.

Consumer AI startup EloElo Group raised $80 million from Hornbill Capital, NBCUniversal, MIT Investment Co, Play Ventures, Kalaari Capital, Waterbridge Ventures and Griffin Gaming Partners.

Healthtech startup Clinics On Cloud raised $12.5 million from Model42.

Peppermint Robotics raised Rs 100 crore (~$10.5 million) from pi Ventures, Crane Venture Partners and Asiana Fund.

Speciality chemicals startup altM raised $10.3 million from Rainmatter by Zerodha, Mela Ventures, Omnivore, Theia Ventures, Aureolis Ventures and Spectrum Impact.

Cleantech startup Two Point O Capital (TW.O) raised $10 million from Transition Venture Capital, Omnivore and angel investors.

Wealthtech startup PowerUp Money raised $10 million from Flourish Ventures, Peak XV Partners, Accel, Blume Ventures, Kae Capital, 8i Ventures and DeVC.

Spacetech startup Cosmoserve Space raised $6 million from Rebright Partners, Aranya Holdings, Naandi Ventures, AUM Ventures and Shakti VC.

item.content:encoded:
Lateral Sparks, the weekly quiz from YourStory, tests your domain knowledge, business acumen, and lateral thinking skills (see the previous edition here). In this 257th edition of the quiz, we present issues tackled by real-life entrepreneurs in their startup journeys.

What would you do if you were in their shoes? At the end of the quiz, you will find out what the entrepreneurs and innovators themselves actually did. Would you do things differently?

Q1: Healthcare

The healthcare system is generally built to treat illness, not to find it early. Where are the entrepreneurial opportunities in preventive care at scale?

Q2: Elder care

Senior citizens today are unwilling to let age define how they live, and are looking for more quality of lifestyle. Where is the business opportunity here?

Q3: Recycling

Efficient recycling of components in used objects can be complex in terms of determining what is inside, how much material can be recovered, and what it will cost to process. How can efficiency be improved here?

Q4: Social insights

Social media is a key discovery and evaluation channel for consumers, but brands don’t leverage these insights well. What can be done to deepen and apply business signals here?

Q5: Construction

Cost overruns, project delays, and disconnected processes remain major challenges in the construction industry. How can technology help here?

Answers!

Congratulations on having come this far! But there’s more to come – answers to these five questions (below), as well as links to articles with more details on the entrepreneurs’ solutions. Happy reading, happy learning – and happy creating!

A1: Healthcare

Founded by Shashank ND, Arpit Garg, and Anshul Khandelwal, healthtech startup Cent is building a vertically integrated preventive health platform. It combines customised hardware, AI-driven radiology, and bioinformatics.

It has reportedly completed 10,000 preventive whole-body scans in three cities since launch, and is targeting 10 million scans by 2035. Read more here about its disease detection capabilities, and its recent fundraise from Blume Ventures and South Park Commons.

A2: Elder care

Founded by Sharad Gadsing, Cradle Of Life focuses on offering seniors four fundamental human aspirations: freedom, purpose, health, and happiness. It enables seniors to learn, contribute and pursue what matters personally.

In terms of design, the residential facilities include a central balcony that extends to every room, layouts with more usable area, and safety through age-friendly furniture. Read more here about its other offerings in healthcare, emergency response, wellness, and community engagement.

A3: Recycling

Attero is an e-waste and battery recycling company that uses AI to speed up decisions across thousands of appliances, suppliers and locations. It processes 200,000 metric tonnes of e-waste and 10,000 metric tonnes of lithium-ion batteries annually, according to Ayush Agarwal, Head of Product.

Its pricing engine combines material intelligence with market intelligence to calculate what the material should cost in a particular market. Read more here about its AI-powered compliance engine that checks documents, reconciles information across records, and flags exceptions.

A4: Social insights

“Brands today are drowning in signals and starved of action,” explains J Venkat, Co-founder of Live2.ai. It monitors conversations across Instagram, TikTok, YouTube, Reddit, X, and review websites.

It integrates trend analysis, influencer-content audits, campaign publishing, and performance measurement for ecommerce. Read more here about how it serves more than 200 brands across the US, Europe and Southeast Asia.

A5: Construction

Founded by Saurav Bhaik and Ankit Sinha, ﻿Tagbin has developed an AI-powered product that integrates architectural drawings, mechanical systems, and project costing. The integrated workflow can be controlled through natural-language prompts.

The platform generates building models, incorporates applicable regulations, and creates construction schedules. Read more here about how it also takes soil-bearing strength and the water table into account while generating foundations and excavation plans.

item.title: Angel One becomes India's second-largest broker by active clients
item.description: The active client base of Angel One for October was 69.98 lakh which was an addition of 2.43 lakh for the month. Zerodha now is in the third spot.
item.content:encoded:
Financial Services firm Angel One has become the country's second-largest stockbroker in terms of active clients, with 69.98 lakh investors on the National Stock Exchange at the end of October, according to the exchange's latest data.

With an active client base of 69.98 lakh, the brokerage now accounts for 14.97% of 4.67 crore active clients across all brokers on the exchange.

The firm added 2.43 lakh net active clients on NSE in October alone.

Its overall client base reached 4.06 crore at the end of October, up 17.4% year-on-year. The company crossed the 4-crore mark during the month after adding nearly 15 lakh clients in the July-September quarter.

Trading activity also picked up in October, with average daily orders rising 19.6% month-on-month to 69.7 lakh. Gross client additions stood at 6.6 lakh, the highest in nine months.

In terms of the number one position, Groww retained its spot with 1.37 crore active clients for the month of October. It also added the highest number of clients at 3.04 lakh during the month and also Groww’s market share was 29.43%.

Bengaluru headquartered Zerodha slipped to third position with overall 67.59 lakh active clients for the month of October which was down by 32,435 from 67.91 lakh in September. This resulted in Zerodha’s market share slipping to 14.46%.

The growth in client numbers of Angel One came alongside an improvement in financial performance.

Angel One's consolidated revenue from operations rose 18.7% year-on-year to Rs 1,427 crore, and net profit grew 58.2% to Rs 335 crore.

Its wealth management assets under management stood at Rs 16,000 crore at the end of the quarter, up 19.1 per cent sequentially.

item.title: Artist Bhagya Ajaikumar explains how good curation balances individual expression and collective vision
item.description: In this photo essay, we showcase the ‘Bhoomi’ exhibition at Venkatappa Art Gallery, along with curator insights.
item.content:encoded:
Launched in 2014, PhotoSparks is a weekly feature from YourStory, with photographs that celebrate the spirit of creativity and innovation. In the earlier 1,030 posts, we featured an art festival, cartoon gallery. world music festival, telecom expo, millets fair, climate change expo, wildlife conference, startup festival, Diwali rangoli, and jazz festival.

The Venkatappa and Swasti art galleries in Bengaluru recently hosted the group exhibition titled Bhoomi (see our coverage of earlier exhibitions at Venkatappa gallery here). It was curated by Bhagya Ajaikumar and Pradeep Kumar DM, with works by around 40 artists.

The Swasti gallery was launched in Bengaluru in 2007 to promote art and raise funds for the HCG Foundation as support for cancer patients. Since 2018, Swasti has also conducted art therapy events for cancer patients and their family members.

Dedicated art space in a hospital setting gives a positive energy to patients and their family members. With that goal in mind, Swasti has been actively involved in organising art shows, camps and workshops, with artists coming from across the country and abroad.

“I am currently planning and working on several exciting projects, both as an artist and a curator. This includes a solo presentation titled THANDAV, featuring my art creations inspired by classical Indian dance,” Ajaikumar tells YourStory.

The exhibition will be presented at the RASA cultural festival at Prestige Auditorium in Bengaluru, January 8-10. 2027. She is also curating the upcoming third International KALA Symposium in Mysuru.

Also Read
Year in Review: The great Indian consumer reset powered by protein, pickleball and micro-dramas

“With the vision of art as a catalyst for healing and development, the symposium is conceived as a creative platform connecting fine art, healthcare philanthropy, and grassroots community development. It will be hosted at Bharath Cancer Hospital,” she adds.

Her gallery is also planning an art activity with paediatric oncology patients to celebrate Children's Day this month. “Another ongoing initiative is the installation of artworks in consultation rooms across our hospitals,” Ajaikumar says.

As trends in Indian contemporary art, she points to the revival of traditional Indian art forms through contemporary interpretations. “Styles such as Madhubani, Gond, Pichwai and Mysore are being explored through acrylics on canvas, square compositions, minimalistic presentations, and unconventional materials,” she observes.

“With increasing competition and the pressure to produce work within shorter periods, many traditional processes are gradually disappearing. Traditional knowledge and techniques should also be respected,” she affirms.

Another exciting development is the transformation of traditional Indian crafts into large-scale contemporary installations. “Some traditional art forms are moving beyond small-format works on paper to large canvases, murals and public installations,” she says.

Indian contemporary art is also responding to changes in social, political and environmental realities. “Many artists are exploring themes of identity, migration, displacement, urbanisation, globalisation, and ecology. They encourage viewers to question and reflect on the world around them,” Ajaikumar observes.

Also Read
Year in Review: Top 10 celebrity-backed ventures of 2025

“I believe this shift is important because art should not merely be decorative. It can communicate ideas, challenge perceptions and create awareness about issues that affect society,” she affirms.

Collectors are increasingly interested in theme-based series rather than isolated, standalone artworks. “Conceptual works, installations, environmentally conscious practices, and works addressing social and women's issues are receiving greater attention,” she adds.

As for tech trends, AI offers digital artists exciting tools and possibilities for experimentation. “However, use of AI also raises important questions about originality, authorship, authenticity and the value of the human hand and imagination in art,” she cautions.

“Another development I find particularly encouraging is the increasing presence of art in public spaces, especially airports. Major airports in cities such as Delhi, Mumbai and Bengaluru are providing opportunities to showcase large-scale artworks and installations,” she observes (see our photo essay on art and design at Bengaluru’s airport here).

With their large spaces, airports can bring art closer to people who may not necessarily visit galleries or museums. “These installations often combine art, architecture, unconventional materials, and multimedia practices. They can transform otherwise functional spaces into engaging cultural environments,” she adds.

The exhibitor lineup in her Bhoomi exhibition includes Meenakshi Chinna Rathod, Meghana Gante Ravish, Nagappa Pradhani, Nikhil R Sharma, Nirmala Kumari CS, Premkumar K, Ranganath Amrad, Revanasiddayya SH, Renuka Markande, SG Vasudev, and Santosh Pattar.

Also Read
Year in review: What 2025’s data tells us about women in India

Akshay Bhat is an emerging contemporary artist from Karnataka whose practice reflects an interest in expressive visual language and contemporary aesthetics. Alka Chavda is a contemporary visual artist whose practice centres on painting and mixed media.

Renuka Markande is an accomplished artist, educator and researcher whose creative practice bridges academic inquiry and contemporary visual expression. Bhagya Ajaikumar explores expressive painting and the emotional possibilities of colour and form.

Hanumanta T frequently draws inspiration from local traditions, landscapes and everyday human interactions, transforming familiar imagery into evocative narratives. Ishwarayya OM explores themes of identity, environment and human resilience.

Manushya explores universal themes of humanity, coexistence and personal identity through painting and interdisciplinary practice. Marishamachar draws inspiration from regional narratives and lived experience, and creates works that resonate with both cultural specificity and universal human concerns.

As a curator of such a diverse exhibition, Ajaikumar particularly likes placing emerging artists alongside established professionals. “This allows them to learn from one another and gain greater exposure,” she explains.

“I believe that an exhibition should offer more than a collection of individual artworks. It should create a meaningful visual and intellectual experience for the viewer,” she says.

Also Read
Year in review: startups that raised big from VCs in 2025

This can be particularly challenging when working with a specific theme. “The curator must establish a meaningful connection between the exhibition's concept and the individual artist's interpretation. There should be a common thread connecting their contributions,” she describes.

“Curators also encourage emerging artists and help them develop their ideas. A carefully curated exhibition can challenge younger artists to think beyond their usual boundaries, experiment with new approaches and raise the quality of their work,” Ajaikumar signs off.

Now what have you done today to pause in your busy schedule and harness your creative side for a better world?

(All photographs taken by Madanmohan Rao on location at Venkatappa Art Gallery.)

item.title: Northern Arc's diversified debt fund hits first close at over Rs 400 Cr
item.description: The 15th private credit fund from Northern Arc Investment Managers targets a Rs 1,500 crore corpus and a 16% XIRR, as its India Impact Fund matures after deploying Rs 1,398 crore.
item.content:encoded:
Northern Arc Investment Managers, the asset management arm of Northern Arc Capital, has announced the first close of its Northern Arc Diversified Debt Fund with commitments of more than Rs 400 crore from institutions, family offices, ultra-high-net-worth individuals (UHNIs) and high-net-worth individuals (HNIs).

The fund is the firm's 15th private credit vehicle. It is a sector-agnostic Category II Alternative Investment Fund (AIF) focused on performing private credit, rated AA (SO) by CareEdge Ratings. It targets a corpus of Rs 1,500 crore, with a greenshoe option of Rs 500 crore that could take it to Rs 2,000 crore. The fund has a five-year tenure and targets a 16% XIRR.

The announcement coincides with the maturity of the Northern Arc India Impact Fund, which channelled global capital into financial inclusion opportunities across India. Over its tenure, the fund supported 60 businesses across credit cycles, with gross deployment of over Rs 1,398 crore at the fund level, backed by UHNIs, family offices, and domestic and global institutional investors.

Commenting on the announcements, Ashish Mehrotra, Managing Director and Chief Executive Officer, Northern Arc Capital, said, "The first close of the Northern Arc Diversified Debt Fund reflects continued investor interest in private credit and its evolving role in sophisticated investment portfolios. The maturity of our Northern Arc India Impact Fund further demonstrates our experience in managing private credit investments across credit cycles. Together, these milestones reinforce our focus on disciplined credit selection, portfolio diversification and risk management.”

He added, “Over the past decade, we have built a diversified private credit platform that has deployed over Rs. 16,500 crores across 15 AIFs and two PMS offerings and served more than 1,500 investors across institutional and wealth segments. As private credit becomes an increasingly strategic allocation for investors, we remain focused on connecting capital with businesses across sectors while creating opportunities for risk-adjusted returns."

Since its inception in 2014, Northern Arc Investment Managers has launched 15 funds, of which seven have fully matured, delivering returns at a weighted average XIRR of over 14.5%, in line with targeted returns, without any extension or principal loss to investors, the company said. It has cumulatively distributed over Rs 10,000 crore of principal and coupon since inception.

Separately, Northern Arc Capital reported a 41% year-on-year growth in consolidated profit after tax to Rs 129 crore in Q2 FY27, while net interest income rose 32% to Rs 425 crore. Lending assets under management grew 34% to Rs 19,003 crore, supported by a 64% rise in direct lending AUM to Rs 12,502 crore, which now accounts for 66% of the overall portfolio. Credit costs improved by 11 basis points to 2.66%."

item.title: MakeMyTrip enters shared mobility space with majority stake in Quick Ride
item.description: MakeMyTrip has acquired the Quick Ride brand and its ride pooling business with a majority stake in this entity.
item.content:encoded:
MakeMyTrip on Friday announced it has acquired a majority stake in 'Quick Ride', a technology-led shared mobility platform, for an undisclosed sum.

The investment provides an opportunity for MakeMyTrip to establish its presence in the shared mobility/ride pooling segment, complementary to the group's existing ground transportation portfolio, the company stated.

Bengaluru-headquartered Quick Ride is a technology-led, asset-light shared mobility platform that connects people travelling along similar routes, enabling affordable ride pooling for everyday commutes.

The 'Quick Ride' brand and its ride pooling business underwent an internal restructuring and are now housed under a new entity, Co Ride Mobility Private Limited. MakeMyTrip has acquired the Quick Ride brand and its ride pooling business with a majority stake in this entity.

Quick Ride's promoters will continue to lead the business. Its erstwhile EV taxi business will remain with the predecessor entity, iDisha Info Labs Private Limited, MakeMyTrip stated.

Rajesh Magow, Co-Founder & Group Chief Executive Officer, MakeMyTrip, said, "As part of our expansion strategy, we have pursued selective strategic partnerships, investments and acquisitions that complement and strengthen our existing business and expand the breadth and depth of our offerings. Ride pooling gives us a presence in high-frequency daily commutes within cities, as well as intercity travel".

Quick Ride will be housed under our ground transport business, and we will bring the learnings from building redBus in India and overseas markets to grow and scale the business, he added.

KNM Rao, Founder and CEO, Quick Ride, said, "Becoming part of the MakeMyTrip group is an important milestone for our team and for the community of users who have placed their trust in us. We look forward to drawing on MakeMyTrip's reach and experience in travel to further scale the business".

In recent years, MakeMyTrip has made acquisitions across travel segments, including Savaari in car rental services, Happay in corporate travel and expense management, Flamingo Transworld in regional group holiday packages and through strategic minority investment in Atlys in visa processing.

item.title: How a Rs 500 Cr bet put Bihar Museum ahead of the Met and Louvre
item.description: How did Bihar Museum enter the global top 10? Shradha Sharma reflects on Nitish Kumar's vision, legal challenges and the persistence behind its success
item.content:encoded:
Bihar Museum in Patna was recently ranked ahead of New York's Metropolitan Museum of Art and the Louvre in Paris. The museum has secured the ninth place on The World's 100 Best Museums 2026, published by German travel guide Worth a Journey. The Met stands tenth and the Louvre 31st. It is the only Indian institution on the list and the highest-ranked museum in Asia. For a museum that opened barely a decade ago, it is a significant achievement. More so because there was a time when the project itself faced serious opposition, with questions raised about its cost, relevance and the way it was being executed.

Reflecting on the recognition in a recent LinkedIn post, YourStory Founder and CEO Shradha Sharma recalled the roles played by two people in getting the museum built: Nitish Kumar, who championed the project as Bihar's Chief Minister, and 1992-batch IAS officer Chanchal Kumar, who was entrusted with its execution. When the state government proposed spending nearly Rs 500 crore on a world-class museum in Patna, the decision attracted criticism. Why should a state struggling with basic infrastructure invest so much in a museum? Who would visit it? Could the money have been better spent elsewhere? According to Sharma, even people within the political establishment questioned the proposal. Nitish Kumar, however, stood by the project, convinced that Bihar needed an institution worthy of its historical and cultural heritage.

This Diwali, this one is for everyone who has ever been written off.
A museum in Patna now ranks above the Met in New York and the Louvre in Paris. The Bihar Museum is 9th on the World’s 100 Best Museums list for 2026 put out by the German travel guide Worth a Journey. The Met is… pic.twitter.com/1sUAvkUqfh

— Shradha Sharma (@SharmaShradha) November 6, 2026

Getting the museum built

The challenges began with the land. According to Sharma, the proposed 13-acre site had seven government bungalows, some occupied by senior officials and a state minister. Getting the occupants to vacate required considerable administrative effort and legal intervention. She also recounted an incident in which men allegedly linked to local politicians entered the construction site demanding subcontracts, prompting police intervention. The museum was designed by Pritzker Prize-winning Japanese architect Fumihiko Maki in collaboration with Mumbai-based architectural firm Opolis, while Larsen & Toubro was selected to construct it. But appointing internationally recognised architects and an established construction company was only part of the challenge. Getting the project completed was another matter.

The museum also faced judicial scrutiny. In June 2015, the Patna High Court, hearing a public interest litigation, criticised the expenditure of approximately Rs 500 crore and questioned the transparency of the contracting process. The court held that the project was not in the public interest but declined to halt construction because the building was nearing completion. Those findings remain an important part of the museum's history. Its international recognition does not erase the questions raised about public spending and governance, although the institution has since gained recognition well beyond Bihar.

Sharma credits much of the execution to Chanchal Kumar, who held the dual responsibility of Secretary of Art and Culture and Secretary of the Building Construction Department.

The arrangement meant that both the museum's cultural vision and its construction came under the same officer. Sharma said she recently read his account of how the museum came together and was struck by how little he spoke about his own contribution. Behind the finished building were years of navigating approvals, land disputes, administrative resistance and the many complications that accompany a large public project. In Sharma's telling, Nitish Kumar's political backing and Chanchal Kumar's persistence were crucial to seeing it through.

A reminder of Bihar's strengths

For Sharma, who grew up in Bihar, the recognition carries a more personal meaning. Few places in India can claim the kind of historical and intellectual inheritance that Bihar possesses. Bodh Gaya is where the Buddha attained enlightenment. Vaishali is closely associated with Mahavira. Ancient Pataliputra was the capital of the Mauryan Empire under Ashoka, while Patna is the birthplace of Guru Gobind Singh. Nalanda and Vikramshila were among the great centres of learning in ancient India. Yet Bihar's present-day image often has little to do with this extraordinary history. Its achievements are celebrated in textbooks, but the state has struggled to build contemporary institutions that attract the same admiration.

Sharma drew on an episode from the Ramayana to explain what the museum means to her. Before Hanuman makes his leap across the ocean to Lanka, Jambavan reminds him of the strength he has forgotten. Bihar, she suggested, needed a similar reminder of what it is capable of achieving. The museum offers one. Its galleries house sculptures, coins, manuscripts and artefacts that bring the region's history to life, including the celebrated Didarganj Yakshi. And now, a German travel publication has placed it among the world's ten best museums, ahead of institutions with far longer histories and international reputations. The ranking is one publication's assessment, but it is nevertheless a significant moment for a museum that faced so many questions during its creation.

item.title: Deepinder Goyal hits back at doctors, defends wearable device Temple
item.description: In a post on X, Goyal said $30 million was invested in building the device, of which he put in $20 million of his personal money.
item.content:encoded:
Eternal founder Deepinder Goyal has posted a series of updates and clarifications on X amid backlash from some Indian doctors who criticised his brain-monitoring wearable Temple. Describing Temple as “an ambitious project”, Goyal gave a detailed explanation on what the team is building.

“The team is delusional enough to think we can build this. And we will,” he wrote on Friday. He also later added that the first 10,000 orders will not have to pay a subscription to use Temple.

Criticising the doctors, he said, "All my emotion last night was directed at a few influencer doctors, who are more influencers than doctors. They did not read our research in detail, and spread twisted facts to call something new a scam. They get views by piling on us."

The open debate started on Thursday when Goyal took to X to defend the device. He said, “First and foremost, a business lesson: if Temple were a scam, and any of what we said weren't true, people would know it in just a few days of using Temple.”

He also said the device features a 14-day no-question return policy. “If the product doesn't work, it fails out of the gate and the company dies before recovering a tenth of its R&D," he said.

Goyal is currently Vice Chairman and Non-Executive Director of Eternal (parent company of Zomato). He is also the founder of healthtech wearable startup Temple and LAT Aerospace.

In the post, Goyal highlighted that $30 million was invested in building the device, including $20 million of his personal money. 

Calling this his purpose, he said it's not about the money. “I have enough of it to last for generations. My incentives are fully aligned with getting the science right. I am not staking a reputation earned over 20 years on making a quick buck.”

Goyal argued that most wearable companies start with internal studies. He referred to Whoop which shipped its fitness band in 2015 but the first published validation happened a few years later. He also added that Temple had a higher standard. "Pre-prints are a step prior to peer reviewed publications, and they are coming up."

Reposing confidence in the product, he said, “We stand by our science and our methods. Each of our claims is easily verifiable by individuals and institutions alike, and you will see a lot of independent studies come up on their own when the device becomes available to use.”

Moreover, he added that this device is a fitness tracker, and wellness device, not a medical device. “If at some point, we clinically validate any of our metrics, we will let you know.”

Dear Concerned Indian Doctors,

I see your rage against Temple on X. I have a few points
to make:

1. First and foremost, a business lesson: if Temple were a scam, and any of what we said weren't true, people would know it in just a few days of using Temple. We have 14-day,…

— Deepinder Goyal (@deepigoyal) November 5, 2026

However, some doctors were not convinced by Goyal’s response.

Responding to Goyal's claim on showing scientific evidence, an X user, who goes by the handle TheLiverdoc, said the Apple Watch Series 11 and Fitbit Sense had shown clinical evidence before launch. Similarly, Samsung Galaxy Watch8 and Watch9 also passed FDA trials prior to release.

"Meanwhile, the Oura Ring 4 and Whoop 4.0 launched as wellness trackers backed by peer-reviewed sleep studies."

To the people disparaging the Indian medical community, please note that we, me included, are not against technological solutions towards improved preventative care. In fact, preventative care is is the heart of medical science.

But, let us not confuse fradulently selling… pic.twitter.com/5riczT3cli

— TheLiverDoc™ (@theliverdoc) November 6, 2026

On X, Dr Rishabh Jain responded saying Goyal shared financial and personal sacrifices but no scientific evidence. "Stop calling legitimate scientific scrutiny 'rage'. You have responded to questions about medical accuracy with investment figures, return policies, personal reputation, and promises of future studies. None of these constitutes scientific validation.”

Criticising the return policy he said, "Subjective satisfaction cannot establish medical accuracy.”

Dr Jain further said that doctors are not against innovation. However the evidence needs to show it. "If Temple delivers what it promises, doctors will be among its biggest supporters."

He also said that science is not a popularity contest, and criticism is not “rage".

Dr Jain also asked for data that can be reviewed by independent researchers.

Dear Temple Team,

Doctors are asking for scientific evidence, not your financial history, personal sacrifices, or business credentials. Stop calling legitimate scientific scrutiny “rage.”

You have responded to questions about medical accuracy with investment figures, return… https://t.co/wh6N0zPypu

— Dr Rishabh Jain (@DrRishabhOnco) November 5, 2026

Temple is a wearable device that tracks blood flow and oxygenation inside the brain. Goyal has not disclosed the price of the device.

In May this year, Goyal announced that the first 100 devices were ready to ship to select founding users and was aimed at athletes, scientists, doctors, founders, creators, and others who could provide feedback on the device. Pre-orders for Temple officially opened in India earlier this month.

In February this year, Temple raised $54 million in its first funding round from friends and family investors, at a valuation of about $190 million.

item.title: Mamaearth parent Honasa's Q2 net profit rises 87%
item.description: The company reported a net profit of Rs 73.24 crore in Q2FY27. Revenue rose 36% YoY to Rs 731.18 crore.
item.content:encoded:
Honasa Consumer, the parent company of beauty & personal care brand Mamaearth, registered an 87% year-on-year (YoY) rise in net profit for the second quarter of the current fiscal, while revenue rose 36% driven by strong growth across categories.

The company reported a net profit of Rs 73.24 crore in Q2FY27, compared with Rs 39.22 crore in the similar period of FY26. Revenue during the quarter was Rs 731.18 crore, compared with Rs 538.06 crore a year ago.

According to Honasa Consumer, the second quarter revenue growth is the highest it has recorded since its public listing in November 2023.

However, sequentially, profit fell from Rs 90.44 crore in the first quarter. Revenue in the first quarter was Rs 755.94 crore.

Honasa also operates the brands Dermacare and Aqualogica.

CEO Varun Alagh said, “At the brand level, each business is writing its own growth story. Mamaearth has sustained its high-teens growth, The Derma Co. continues to grow profitably. Our Younger Brands grew over 45% YoY, reflecting highlighting the potential of our emerging portfolio.”

He added that each brand has a distinct consumer, proposition and opportunity and the goal is to build a sustainable business in each category.

The omnichannel channel retailer noted that its offline business saw growth, with general trade expanding to over 3.2 lakh outlets and modern trade (large-format retail outlets) recording a 40% YoY growth in offtake.

“As we enter the next phase of growth, we will continue to push the boundaries of innovation, deepen our presence in core categories, and make our products accessible to more consumers across channels,” said Ghazal Alagh, CIO & Co-founder, Honasa Consumer.

For the six months of the fiscal year, the company reported a revenue of Rs 1,487.13 crore, a YoY growth of 31%. The net profit for the period was Rs 163.69 crore, a YoY rise of 103%.
